clue.text: Guardian's put through edited parody, being sorry?

indicators.note: one piece is pushed through the middle of the other, so it ends up sitting inside it
an edited text has been reworked, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

parts.note: from the point of view of the paper this clue runs in, something that belongs to the Guardian is 'ours'

explanation.surface: A reader complains that the Guardian has run a botched parody, and asks whether anyone is apologising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edited' sits between parody and being, yet both words are rearranged into IBEGYPARDON; 'Guardian's' means 'ours' from the paper's own point of view.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a formal apology, what a person says when they are sorry, and the question mark allows the conversational form.

clue.text: One's opening is always repeated twice

parts.note: ay, or aye, is an old poetic word meaning ever or forever

indicators.note: the piece is said once and then repeated twice more, giving three goes in all

parts.note: ay, or aye, is an old poetic word meaning ever or forever

explanation.surface: A statement that something is always said twice, as if describing a habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repeated twice' means said, then repeated twice: ISAY three times in all.
explanation.definitionFit: The triple exclamation is the stock opening line of a British music-hall comedian, so it is a comic's start to a gag.

clue.text: Nude dancing? Take a little Peter Pan out!

indicators.note: letters that are dancing are jumping about, so the word nude is reshuffled
only a small piece of the name is taken, its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone is told to remove a little Peter Pan from the stage during a nude dance number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter Pan' looks like one name, but Peter supplies a letter and 'Pan out' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan out is to turn out or result in a certain way, the same as the phrasal verb meaning finish in a particular state.

clue.text: Leader having dropped right down, scrutinises excuses rather!

indicators.note: in a down clue the first letter falls all the way to the bottom, becoming the last letter of the whole

parts.note: to scrutinise something is to eye it closely
pleas are excuses offered in mitigation

explanation.surface: A puzzling line about a leader who has fallen and is examining people's excuses.
explanation.walkthrough: EYES + PLEAS gives EYESPLEAS; its opening E moves to the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: Rather! is an old-fashioned eager acceptance of an offer, the same enthusiastic agreement as the polite two-word reply.

clue.text: Diabolical ruses employed to get around North Dakota, "The Altogether State"

indicators.note: the shuffled word goes around the abbreviation, holding it inside
something diabolical is terribly done, so the word ruses is jumbled

parts.note: ND is the postal abbreviation for the US state of North Dakota

explanation.surface: Some devilish tricks are used to get around a US state, which has a joke nickname.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diabolical' makes URESS from ruses. 'State' looks like a US state like North Dakota, but it is a state of being: in the altogether means naked.
explanation.definitionFit: In the altogether means naked, so the state of being in the altogether is nakedness, a state of being unclothed.

clue.text: Quite esurient, rather like a 1962 Oscar winner?

parts.note: Gregory Peck won the Best Actor Oscar in 1962 for To Kill a Mockingbird
the suffix -ish means somewhat like or rather

explanation.surface: Someone fairly hungry is compared, oddly, with a Hollywood Oscar winner.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient is a rare word for hungry, and being slightly hungry is the colloquial British sense of feeling a bit empty.

clue.text: A low approach shot towards the hole, presumably to come second

definitions.text: A low approach shot towards the hole
definitions.meaning: in golf, a low shot that bounces and rolls along the ground up to the green
a runner-up comes second, so jokingly the verb for what a runner-up does

explanation.surface: A golfer's short low shot and the idea of finishing second, together like a tournament report.
explanation.definitionFit: The golfing term is standard; the second sense is a whimsical back-formation from runner-up, hence presumably.

clue.text: Such as XL and I zero in on nameless poetry

indicators.note: N is short for name, so nameless removes an N

parts.note: taken as written before its N goes

indicators.note: the two short pieces go inside the longer string

parts.note: verses are lines of poetry
Z can stand for zero, as in the shorthand for a nil score

explanation.surface: XL and I zero in on poetry that has no name: an odd hunt for anonymous verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nameless' removes the N of 'on', since N is short for name. XL looks like Roman 40, but here it is the clothing size.
explanation.definitionFit: XL is the clothing label for extra large, an example of a size above the standard range.

clue.text: A range of Italian desserts

indicators.note: the answer is made of letters taken from inside the following words

explanation.surface: A menu offering a selection of Italian desserts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A range of' reads as an assortment, but 'A range' is the definition and the answer sits across ItaliAN DESserts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes are a South American mountain range, the longest continental chain in the world.

clue.text: Mother, perhaps, is unable to do/does dressing

indicators.note: the outer word clothes the inner one, wrapping around it

parts.note: does are female deer
can't means is unable to do something

explanation.surface: A cryptic remark about mother and an inability to do the dressing, as if at a clumsy salad prep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shall I be mother?' is British slang for offering to pour the tea, so a mother is someone who pours. 'does' is the plural of doe, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: One who pours liquid from one vessel to another, which is what 'mother' does at the British tea table.

clue.text: Does such an attraction have no point? One, actually, for each side

parts.note: goalless means without a goal or aim, with no point to it
a draw is something that attracts people, a crowd-puller

explanation.surface: A question whether some attraction is pointless, followed by a remark that each side gets one.
explanation.walkthrough: In football a match with no goals still gives each team one league point, hence 'One, actually'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nil-nil football result earns each team a single league point, so it is literally one point for each side.

clue.text: Back at university, London one, after writer's urge to act

indicators.note: the remaining pieces follow the writer's contribution

parts.note: the setter is the writer, so writer's means I'm, I am

indicators.note: back means the short word is turned round

parts.note: up means in residence at a university, a British usage
the LSE, the London School of Economics, is a university in London

explanation.surface: A writer returns to a London university and feels a sudden urge to act.
explanation.walkthrough: UP reverses to PU; I'M + PU + LSE gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An impulse is a sudden spontaneous urge, a drive to do something without forethought.

clue.text: Paint not thinly applied is gone in one second

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the word for gone sits inside the word for second

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
past means gone by

explanation.surface: Thickly applied paint dries away in a second.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the painting technique of laying paint on thickly so brush strokes stand out from the surface.

clue.text: Lining of coat's easily lost

indicators.note: a lining sits inside a garment, so the answer lies inside these words

explanation.surface: The lining of a coat comes away easily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lining' suggests the garment, but it points inside coAT'S EAsily; 'lost' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at sea is to be confused or bewildered, not knowing what to do: an idiom for being lost.

clue.text: Very posh, a woman's in Kent, say

indicators.note: the three short pieces go inside the word for very

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
U is the label for upper-class usage, posh
per means a, as in so much a head
her refers to a woman; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A very posh woman lives in the English county of Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kent' looks like the county south-east of London but is Clark Kent, Superman's everyday identity.
explanation.definitionFit: Clark Kent is the mild-mannered alter ego of Superman, so he is an example of a costumed crime-fighter.

clue.text: Hertz clients taken out for some food

indicators.note: taken out in the sense of taken apart, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Hz is the symbol for hertz, the unit of frequency

explanation.surface: Customers of the Hertz car hire firm are taken out for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hertz' looks like the car rental company but gives its unit symbol HZ, shuffled with CLIENTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A schnitzel is a breaded escalope of veal or pork, a dish of Austrian origin.

clue.text: Rip centre of kitchen out today and fly!

indicators.note: ripping something up tears it apart, so the letters are rearranged
the centre of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter
out signals that the named letter is removed

parts.note: now means at the present day

explanation.surface: An instruction to tear out the middle of the kitchen and take a flight today.
explanation.walkthrough: KITCHEN loses its centre C, leaving KITHEN, rearranged to INTHEK. 'fly' is the adjective, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Fly is British slang for knowing and shrewd, the same as being well informed about what is going on.

clue.text: Showing admiration, Enigmatist is doing Mr Rusbridger's job!

parts.note: Enigmatist is the setter, so 'Enigmatist is' means I'm
Alan Rusbridger was editor of the Guardian, a press editor; press and ed are taken from that phrase
Alan Rusbridger was editor of the Guardian, a press editor; press and ed are taken from that phrase

explanation.surface: The setter claims, admiringly, to be doing the editor's job.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Rusbridger edited the Guardian from 1995 to 2015.
explanation.definitionFit: Being impressed means feeling admiration, so the past participle describes someone showing respect.

clue.text: Pessimistic canon's portion of ground cabbage salad

parts.note: a sod is a piece of turf, a portion of grassy ground
slaw is coleslaw, shredded cabbage salad

explanation.surface: A gloomy churchman's share of a plot of ground and some coleslaw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canon' looks like a clergyman but means a rule or law.
explanation.definitionFit: The rule that whatever can go wrong will go wrong is a gloomy principle, a pessimist's law.

clue.text: Arty male performer excited 70% of Sun readers

indicators.note: excited particles move about, so the letters are rearranged
seven letters out of ten are kept, dropping the last three

explanation.surface: An artistic male entertainer has stirred up most readers of the tabloid Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: SUN READERS has ten letters; 70% keeps SUNREAD, rearranged. The Sun is a British tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: A danseur is a male ballet dancer, a performer in an art form.

clue.text: Liking condition No 1 to become No 3

indicators.note: the letter in first position moves to third position

parts.note: a state is a condition

explanation.surface: A cryptic rule about a condition being demoted from first to third place, as in a league table.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste for something is a liking or preference for it.

clue.text: Feather-brain needs help to catch leggy bird

indicators.note: the word for help grabs the bird and holds it inside

parts.note: aid means help
the rhea is a long-legged flightless bird of South America

explanation.surface: A dimwit needs help catching a long-legged bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feather-brain' plays on the bird theme but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Feather-brain and its synonym both describe a silly, empty-headed person.

clue.text: Self-willed velocity witnessed in dash

indicators.note: the letter is seen inside the other word

parts.note: elan is dash or flair
v is the symbol for velocity in physics

explanation.surface: A wilful burst of speed seen in a sprint.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvan is an old adjectival form relating to elves, and elves were thought mischievous and wayward, hence wilful.

clue.text: Unnecessarily wily fleeing rocks

indicators.note: something fleeing runs away, so these letters leave the longer word

parts.note: needlessly means unnecessarily
sly means wily

explanation.surface: Someone wily runs off for no good reason.
explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are a line of chalk rocks off the Isle of Wight, on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Needles are a famous group of chalk stacks, an example of rocks.

clue.text: Correct reasoning traps soldier in mountain pass heading north

indicators.note: the outer word holds the soldier caught inside it
in a down clue, going north means reading upwards, so the word is backwards

parts.note: a col is a pass between mountain peaks
a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: Sound reasoning traps a soldier in a pass as he heads north.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'heading north' reads the pass upwards, giving LOC, before 'traps' puts the soldier inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is the science of valid reasoning, the principles of correct inference.

clue.text: Honey and lemon's first sipped by loathsome author

parts.note: mel is the Latin for honey, seen in pharmacy

indicators.note: the letter is taken into the other word, as if drunk

parts.note: vile means loathsome

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Honey and lemon being sipped by an unpleasant writer, like a cold remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman Melville was the American novelist who wrote Moby-Dick.

clue.text: Not quite full backing for Queen and Country

indicators.note: backing means the word is read backwards
not quite full means the last letter is missing

parts.note: Regina is Latin for queen, seen in R as a royal cipher

explanation.surface: A half-hearted show of support for Queen and Country.
explanation.walkthrough: REGINA loses its last letter to give REGIN, which reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: Niger is a landlocked West African state.

clue.text: Declaration from elocutionist who won crown, movingly taking in bow

indicators.note: moving the letters around rearranges them

explanation.surface: The winner of a crown makes a speech and takes a bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking in' tells us BOW joins the fodder WHO WON CROWN; all the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyming phrase is a traditional exercise used by elocution teachers to practise vowel sounds.
